title: What We Have Measured
summary: A measured outcome is a claim supported by a recorded quantity, a defined instrument or method, stated conditions, and a figure. Creative Navy's measured evidence includes live deployment metrics, product analytics, controlled tests, eye tracking, field observation, client-measured operational data, a regulatory approval outcome, and small controlled prototype comparisons with explicit limitations.
keyFacts: Measured outcomes exclude client-reported claims without disclosed measurement methodology, directional observations without quantification, and inferred outcomes.
The eToro entry is the only randomised controlled comparison on the page, with a simultaneous user-level holdout.
Gexcon, Triopsis, Beissbarth, Polymatica, Tetra / Prism, and several other entries use live system, deployment, product analytics, or client-owned measurement.
Torqeedo, Typewise, Stromer, Streetec, Raymarine, Squaremind, and the maritime VTS engagement include Creative Navy-run or Creative Navy-designed behavioural measurement under stated conditions.

CDR Foodlab and Squaremind include mixed-basis before and after comparisons where the pre-redesign baseline is client-reported and the post-redesign evidence is Creative Navy-measured or Creative Navy-run.
Kardion's FDA approval is included as a verifiable regulatory judgement, not as an operational performance metric.
Petrol station operator and visioncheckout entries are measurement baselines that grounded design decisions, not post-redesign outcome claims.
Raymarine and maritime VTS entries are descriptive controlled comparisons on prototypes, not production deployment measurements.
Schone Airspace Group, AIT, MDU, Assemblio, Oceaneering, KISPE, Egma, and handheld C2 material are excluded for stated evidence-category reasons.

bodySections.heading: Definition of measured outcomes in Creative Navy evidence standards
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

A measured outcome is an outcome where a specific quantity was recorded using a defined instrument or method, under conditions that are stated and relevant to real use. In Creative Navy's evidence standards, measured outcomes exclude client-reported outcomes without a disclosed measurement methodology, directional observations without quantification, and outcomes inferred from system structure rather than tested against it.

Measured outcomes can be interrogated because they carry a baseline, a method, a condition, and a figure. Within this category, evidence still differs in causal strength. A randomised controlled comparison isolates the design change more cleanly than a before and after comparison. A field measurement in live operation has stronger ecological validity than a laboratory-only task, but may provide weaker causal isolation.

bodySections.heading: Evidence strength differs within the measured category
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy's strongest causal example is eToro, where a randomised controlled A/B test compared a redesigned treatment experience against a simultaneous holdout from the same population. Most other measured outcomes on this page rely on before and after comparison, product analytics, deployment tracking, structured usability testing, eye tracking, or field observation.

Before and after comparisons remain useful when their evidential basis is explicit. Enhesa and Gericke are cited in the category definition as examples where attribution confidence comes from a confirmed no-other-changes window, although their detailed entries are not included on this page. UNICEF and Gericke are cited as examples where confidence comes from metrics already owned and operated by the client. Gexcon, Torqeedo, and Stromer are cited as examples where measurement occurred in real operating conditions.

Some before and after comparisons are mixed-basis. In CDR Foodlab and Squaremind, the post-redesign evidence was produced through Creative Navy measurement or Creative Navy-run testing, while the pre-redesign baseline was client-reported background. Those comparisons are meaningful only when both figures travel with their evidence basis.

bodySections.heading: Gexcon deployment tracking measured operational change in industrial CFD software
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Gexcon measured four operational metrics across real deployment locations after Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design engagement. These were operational measurements from the live system, not usability test results.

The measured changes were: time to first successful simulation reduced from 4 days to 6 hours, a 93% reduction; configuration errors per simulation reduced from 5–8 to 1–2; corrective load per error reduced from 4–6 hours to approximately 20 minutes; and active users per team increased from 1 to 3–4.

The evidential basis is client-measured deployment tracking by Gexcon across deployment locations. The data came from live operational use, not controlled test conditions.

bodySections.heading: Triopsis product analytics measured productivity in live workforce management SaaS
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Triopsis measured three productivity metrics through product analytics from real users operating the live system in professional field conditions. Job discovery was 62% faster, job sequence optimisation was 83% faster, and weekly planning was 58% faster.

The evidential basis is product analytics from deployed production software. The figures are not from a controlled experiment, and the claim is limited to measured usage data from real operational conditions.

bodySections.heading: Torqeedo combined a controlled maritime HMI experiment with eye tracking at sea
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Torqeedo measured two outcomes under real maritime conditions during sea trial testing with professional captains. Energy state identification was 50% faster than the legacy interface in a controlled experiment with 24 subjects. Glance reduction during manoeuvres was measured using eye tracking in actual sea trials with 7 subjects.

The precise glance counts are not published. The supportable claim is that the direction of glance reduction was measured rather than inferred. The conditions included vibration, night operations, vessel movement, and cold water glare, which are stated as conditions of professional maritime work rather than laboratory reproductions.

bodySections.heading: Typewise measured keyboard error rate and typing speed against iOS native keyboard
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy ran a controlled experiment with 60 users toward the end of the Typewise engagement. The test measured the Typewise mobile keyboard against the iOS native keyboard as the explicit baseline.

The error rate was halved compared to the iOS native keyboard. Typing speed increased from 38 WPM to 47 WPM. The evidential basis is Creative Navy-run controlled testing during the engagement, not client-reported evidence. The testing setup was designed to create realistic pressure conditions so that qualitative feedback could be gathered alongside the measurements.

bodySections.heading: eToro is the portfolio example of a randomised controlled comparison
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
After Creative Navy redesigned eToro's landing, buy, and explore surfaces, eToro measured the impact through a randomised controlled A/B test. This is the only entry on this page with a simultaneous control arm rather than a before and after comparison.

Discovery-to-trade conversion rate changed from 5.1% in the control arm to 7.4% in the treatment arm, a 45% relative uplift. Median time to first trade changed from 11.8 minutes in the control arm to 8.6 minutes in the treatment arm, a 27% reduction.

The experiment served the redesigned surfaces to a randomised treatment group while a statistically matched holdout continued on the existing experience. Assignment was randomised and stable at the user level, not the session level, to prevent cross-exposure contamination. The split was 50/50, with 1,625 users in each arm. A 2-week stabilisation window was excluded, after which the primary measurement window ran for 6 weeks.

The evidential basis is client-measured data from eToro's own analytics stack, using eToro's predefined success metrics, success thresholds, 72-hour conversion attribution window, and cross-surface session stitching definitions. The design of the experiment isolates the interface change from market movement because both arms were exposed to the same market conditions over the same period. Both figures cleared eToro's predefined statistical-significance thresholds.

The figures must be framed as improved decision coherence, not increased trading volume. The time-to-trade reduction occurred without an increase in early-session drop-off and without a reduction in exploration depth. The source framing states that users converged faster and explored as much, indicating reduced cognitive friction in resolving uncertainty rather than impulsive trading. Without those conditions, the figures would be unsafe under MiFID II financial-promotion and SEC/FINRA fair-balance expectations.

bodySections.heading: Tetra / Prism client-measured adoption and NPS sit near the measured boundary
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Tetra measured mobile app adoption and web platform NPS before and after the redesigned app and web platform. Mobile app adoption increased from 12% to 64% over the year following the redesigned app launch. Web platform NPS improved from 72% to 85%, with the second measurement taken approximately 4 months after the new web design launched.

The evidential basis is client-measured data from Tetra. Creative Navy did not independently verify the figures. These outcomes sit at the boundary between measured and client-reported categories because they were produced by defined measurement at defined points in time, but by the client rather than independently by Creative Navy.

bodySections.heading: Beissbarth field measurement recorded shorter calibration time in production deployments
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Beissbarth measured calibration time per vehicle across 8 real production deployment locations. Calibration time reduced from 18 minutes to 12 minutes.

The evidential basis is client-measured field data from production deployments, not a usability test result. Beissbarth directionally confirmed a reduction in repeated measurements, but the precise figure was not shared with Creative Navy and should not be stated.

bodySections.heading: Polymatica product analytics measured independent task completion across two releases
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Polymatica measured independent task completion through product analytics across three points. The baseline was 2% of users completing tasks independently. After release 1, the figure was 40%. After release 2, the figure was 56%.

The evidential basis is product analytics. The three-point longitudinal record across two design releases gives this entry more continuity than a single before and after UX outcome.

bodySections.heading: Kardion FDA approval is a verifiable regulatory judgement, not an operational metric
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The Kardion MCS Controller received FDA approval. The submitted design passed the regulatory evaluation with no design changes required.

This is a distinct type of entry on this page. It is not a before and after productivity figure and not an operational performance metric. It is a documented and verifiable regulatory judgement that the design met the human factors requirements of FDA submission, a condition requiring demonstrable usability evidence and structured usability engineering documentation.

bodySections.heading: Elsner combined published ergonomics research with formal usability testing
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
For the Elsner smart home controller Cala Touch KNX, touch target sizing was grounded in published ergonomics research by Herbert A. Colle and Keith J. Hiszem from 2004. The research stated that touch targets should be a minimum of 13mm and that accuracy improves only to approximately 22mm.

Creative Navy applied the research in formal usability testing with 12 subjects in a structured testing session. The testing confirmed navigation legibility, temperature control comprehension, and touch target accuracy under standing-height, varying-luminance conditions.

bodySections.heading: Petrol station operator measurement was an operational baseline for POS concept evaluation
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy measured operational data during field observation for an embedded POS and forecourt systems engagement. The recorded baseline included 84 transactions per hour at peak rate, a 7-minute complex transaction duration before redesign, and 532 transactions coded by type and complexity.

The evidential basis is Creative Navy-recorded structured field observation: 40 hours of observation and 24 interviews. These figures are not claims about post-redesign change. They are the measurement base used to evaluate 16 alternative POS architectures.

bodySections.heading: visioncheckout measurement was a field baseline, not a redesign outcome
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy conducted field research for visioncheckout at six locations across three organisations over five days, observing 563 interactions with the system in live operation. Transaction durations were measured with a clock during observation rather than estimated or self-reported. The research also included interviews with 34 users and 13 catering staff.

Measured standard transaction durations were approximately 13 seconds at a chemical manufacturer's staff restaurant, approximately 11 seconds at an automotive supplier's canteen, and approximately 25 seconds at a large public leisure venue with several restaurants. Unusual transactions, including removing lids, a guest unable to find a card, and errors, ran to more than 20 seconds. At the leisure venue, roughly two thirds of observed transactions were multi-tray, with two to four trays common.

When an error occurred, resolution took one to four minutes. During that time, three to twelve people could not check out. The three to twelve people figure is an observed consequence of a measured duration, not an independently counted figure.

The constraints are part of the evidence. The programme involved one researcher and five days. The timings measure the system being replaced, not the redesign. The number 563 is the engagement's observation figure and is the only observation count that should be used.

bodySections.heading: CDR Foodlab has a mixed-basis task completion comparison
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy measured task completion time on the shipped CDR Foodlab product after the redesign. The post-redesign average task completion time was 3.4 minutes, measured by Creative Navy with 14 users on the final shipped product.

The pre-redesign average task completion time was 9 minutes. That figure was client-reported by CDR Foodlab from internal measurement and was not Creative Navy-measured.

The before and after comparison indicates a 62% reduction, but it is valid only as a mixed-basis claim. The post-redesign figure meets the measured standard. The pre-redesign figure is client-reported. Both labels must travel with the comparison.

CDR Foodlab also commissioned an independent third party to survey usability satisfaction before and after the redesign. The survey used an identical instrument across both rounds and drew from the same population: 68 respondents before redesign and 76 respondents one year after deployment. Satisfaction changed from 72% to 93%. That survey belongs with client-reported outcomes because Creative Navy did not design or conduct the measurement, even though the independent third-party administration and identical instrument make it methodologically stronger than many client-reported outcomes.

bodySections.heading: Stromer combined three usability test rounds, eye tracking, and public app store data
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy designed and ran structured usability testing before and after the Stromer redesign, then conducted a two-year longitudinal follow-up using the same test structure. Ten participants rode the Stromer bike for 3 days each on real routes in Munich and surrounding countryside. Every issue was logged with a 4-level severity rating: interference, annoyance, issue needing user intervention, and critical issue.

In Round 1 before redesign, warnings accounted for approximately 30% of all issues rated as requiring user intervention. In Round 2 after redesign, 10 participants used the same bikes, same routes, and same logging protocol; warnings did not appear on the issues list at any severity level. In Round 3, two years after the redesign, warnings remained absent from the issues list.

For 5 participants, Creative Navy measured glance behaviour using eye tracking equipment during actual riding on the same routes. Average glance duration changed from 4.32 seconds before redesign to 1.89 seconds after redesign. Glance frequency per kilometre was 18% lower after redesign.

The 4.32-second pre-redesign figure exceeded the 2-second threshold established by road safety research as the point at which near-crash and crash risk doubles, cited as Klauer et al. 2006, NHTSA Report No. DOT HS 810 594, and NHTSA Driver Distraction Guidelines Phase 1, 2013. ISO 15007:2020 defines the standard methodology for measuring driver visual behaviour in relation to transport information and control systems, and the Stromer measurement methodology was aligned with this standard. The standards are formally defined for four-wheeled vehicles; the source states that the threshold and principle apply directly to embedded displays used during riding.

Stromer's app store average rating changed from 3.2 before the engagement to 4.1 after relaunch. This is public app store data and independently verifiable, distinct from the Creative Navy-run usability testing and eye tracking. Creative Navy also analysed a public review corpus in which usability mentions in negative reviews changed from 54% to 8%, based on 200 pre-engagement and 59 post-relaunch reviews; the smaller post-relaunch sample should be noted when citing those percentages.

bodySections.heading: Squaremind post-redesign usability testing used an ecological two-site protocol
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy designed and co-conducted post-redesign Squaremind usability testing in two locations with an independent dermatologist hired by Creative Navy. The protocol involved 29 users across London and Paris, with age-stratified samples. Participants received a free measurement as they would in a real clinic and received no researcher guidance during the process.

The primary measure was binary completion: whether the user completed the full scan with the report issued by the device without external intervention. Secondary measures were total scan time and recovery time for users who got stuck.

Post-redesign, 27 of 29 users completed the scan independently. Twelve users got stuck during the flow; all 12 recovered and completed without external intervention. Recovery time was 2 to 4 minutes per user, with older users tending toward the longer end. Failure points and contributing factors were catalogued by step across all 29 sessions.

The pre-redesign baseline is client-reported background from Squaremind's own pre-engagement test with 14 users, where 2 users completed. Of the 12 who failed, 8 primarily aged 45–65 got stuck within the first minute, and 4 primarily aged 20–35 got stuck around the 3-minute mark. This baseline establishes the scale of improvement but is not Creative Navy-generated evidence.

bodySections.heading: Streetec measured task completion on the production product installed in a real car
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy designed the Streetec test protocol, ran both sessions, and analysed the results. Streetec prepared the vehicle and site logistics and recruited participants. Testing used the production kntrl 2 product installed in a car rather than a prototype in a laboratory.

Two testing sessions were run with 32 participants: 13 in Munich, all tuning enthusiasts and car owners, and 19 at a trade fair in Spain, with a mixed group of roughly 25% owners and enthusiasts, 40% dealers, 30% installers, and 5% other. Each participant attempted three tasks with no instruction. Completion and time taken were recorded, followed by a 15-minute debrief capturing opinions and subjective impressions.

The supportable measured claim is that all 32 participants completed all three tasks unassisted and performed in line with expectations. No completion percentage, specific time, mean, or baseline comparison should be stated. The debrief findings are subjective impressions from a 15-minute conversation.

bodySections.heading: Raymarine measured behavioural comparisons on a prototype and fixed scenario fixture
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy designed the Raymarine test protocols, moderated all 24 sessions, and analysed the results. Raymarine supplied the physical bench mockup. The comparisons were paired and counterbalanced within participants, with task wording, target data, and starting states held constant.

The findings describe operator behaviour on a prototype against a fixed scenario fixture. They are not measures of radio performance, real-world calling accuracy, or outcomes at sea. Twenty-four sessions were completed by 18 distinct people, because 6 participants took part in two rounds.

In the control-model comparison, wrong domain activations were 6 of 8 under the contextual model and 0 of 8 under the fixed model on both the retune and recovery tasks. Unassisted completion was 6 of 8 contextual and 8 of 8 fixed, with both prompted completions under the contextual model. Median retune time was 9.70 seconds contextual and 3.25 seconds fixed. Median recovery after interruption was 14.05 seconds contextual and 6.70 seconds fixed. The fixed-role model removed a class of error and cost 2.30 seconds of median target browsing: 6.25 seconds contextual against 8.55 seconds fixed.

In the confirmation comparison, wrong recipient submissions were 2 of 8 under immediate calling and 0 of 8 under confirmation. Four of 8 made an initial wrong target selection under immediate calling, while 2 of 8 submitted one. All 3 initial selection errors under the confirmation condition were detected and corrected at the confirmation screen before any request was sent. The confirmation step cost 5.85 seconds and two and a half interactions, with median completion 17.95 seconds immediate against 23.80 seconds confirmed and median physical actions 6.0 against 8.5.

Status comprehension was 3 of 8 correct with a generic success surface and 8 of 8 with explicit transaction states. Five participants interpreted a generic call-sent message as meaning the other vessel had responded or that voice communication was already available.

Scenario probes remain descriptive within scenario. Seven of 8 resumed the interrupted task unassisted, with median resumption time 12.60 seconds across all 8 attempts and 12.00 seconds across the 7 unassisted recoveries. Seven of 8 recognised and correctly classified the risk event, with median recognition latency 3.60 seconds and a range of 2.1 to 8.2 seconds. Eight of 8 activated the man-overboard function correctly. Seven of 8 distinguished an unavailable AIS receiver from a genuinely empty traffic picture. Eight of 8 retained local voice and digital calling after the chartplotter was disconnected.

The caveat is material: Raymarine measurements were conducted on a prototype before the product was built, against a fixed synthetic fixture, with 8 participants per round and no significance testing. The records describe descriptive within-scenario comparisons from a small purposive sample, not population estimates. No live transmission occurred and zero live distress calls were made.

bodySections.heading: Maritime VTS measured a counterbalanced paired comparison against the legacy product
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy measured a counterbalanced paired study for a European vendor of maritime traffic monitoring, inland navigation, and communications software for port authorities, coastal administrations, and waterway operators. Eight professional VTS operators and supervisors completed four matched tasks in both the existing interface and the redesigned prototype.

Median time to first answer fell by 42.3% on vessel identification, 34.2% on alert prioritisation, and 32.2% on handover retrieval. Correct first answers rose from 23 of 32 to 32 of 32. Correct recognition of historical replay rose from 5 of 8 to 8 of 8.

The per-task record is separate and must stay separate. Vessel identification changed from 61.5 seconds legacy median first answer to 35.5 seconds on the prototype, with correct first answers 6 of 8 and then 8 of 8. Alert prioritisation changed from 80.5 seconds to 53.0 seconds, with correct first answers 6 of 8 and then 8 of 8. Handover retrieval changed from 107.0 seconds to 72.5 seconds, with correct first answers 6 of 8 and then 8 of 8. Replay recognition was untimed and scored only on whether the participant recognised that the picture was historical.

Four participants took the legacy interface first and four took the prototype first. Task data was reset between conditions, with the same decision prompts and stop rule. The study produced 64 condition-level observations and published the full participant-by-condition correctness matrix and raw paired time arrays, reproducing each median arithmetically.

The framing is mandatory. This was Creative Navy-measured under controlled conditions. Eight participants completed four of the seven operator journeys using sanitised training scenarios on a design prototype, not a production installation. Six of the 8 had taken part in earlier research or testing. The time measure was time to a first submitted answer regardless of whether that answer was correct. The study reports no significance test, no confidence interval, and no power calculation. The three percentages must not be averaged or combined into one figure.

bodySections.heading: What the measured category excludes
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy's measured category does not include client-reported outcomes without a disclosed measurement methodology, even when those outcomes are commercially significant. Those outcomes belong with the client-reported evidence standard.

Creative Navy's measured category does not include directional outcomes observed without quantification. Those belong with observed but not quantified evidence. It also does not include outcomes inferred from the structural logic of a system, which belong with inferred evidence.

Creative Navy's measured category does not include outcomes Creative Navy explicitly does not claim, including compliance certifications Creative Navy did not produce and commercial results whose causal attribution would overstate the design's role.

Creative Navy's measured category also excludes conformance figures, acceptance-check figures, and fidelity statements. The AIT, MDU, and Assemblio fidelity verifications and the two component-adoption claims belong with verified without measuring evidence because fidelity is not performance.

Schone Airspace Group figures do not appear in this measured category because Schone measured no outcomes. Its figures are design-conformance results and calculated design properties: 32 of 36 checks, ten contrast ratios, and 28 UI specification checks.

Oceaneering material does not appear because nothing in that engagement was measured. Its client-confirmed fidelity statement is client-reported, not a Creative Navy verification. KISPE, MDU, and Egma material are also excluded for the stated reasons that nothing was measured, nothing was tested or observed with users, or no stated method supports the heatmap as a measured result.

Handheld C2 material remains excluded because Creative Navy designed and ran a NASA-TLX workload assessment against the tier the specification labelled a hypothesis, but no participants, conditions, or result are recorded. No result from that engagement enters the measured category unless the result is recovered.

strongClaims: A measured outcome is a specific quantity recorded using a defined instrument or method under stated conditions relevant to real use.
The eToro entry is the strongest causal structure on the page because it used a randomised controlled A/B test with a simultaneous user-level holdout.
Torqeedo measured faster energy state identification in a controlled experiment with 24 subjects and measured glance reduction through eye tracking with 7 subjects in sea trials.
Typewise testing measured a halved error rate and typing speed increase from 38 WPM to 47 WPM against the iOS native keyboard.
Stromer has Creative Navy-run structured usability testing across three rounds and eye tracking in real riding conditions, with average glance duration changing from 4.32 seconds to 1.89 seconds.
Kardion's FDA approval is a verifiable regulatory outcome, not an operational performance metric.
Raymarine measurements are descriptive behavioural comparisons on a prototype and fixed scenario fixture, not measures of radio performance or outcomes at sea.

The maritime VTS engagement is a within-participant counterbalanced comparison with stronger causal isolation than before and after entries but weaker external validity than deployment or sea trial data.
weakerClaims: Gexcon measured operational improvements across deployment locations, including time to first successful simulation reducing from 4 days to 6 hours.
CDR Foodlab's 62% task-time reduction comparison is mixed-basis: post-redesign 3.4 minutes Creative Navy-measured, pre-redesign 9 minutes client-reported.
limitations: Measured outcomes on this page differ in causal strength; not every measured result supports a strict causal claim.
Most measured outcomes are before and after comparisons rather than randomised controlled comparisons.
Several entries are client-measured rather than independently verified by Creative Navy.
CDR Foodlab and Squaremind include mixed-basis before and after comparisons where the pre-redesign baseline is client-reported.
Petrol station operator and visioncheckout entries are measurement baselines that grounded design decisions, not post-redesign outcome claims.
Kardion's FDA approval is a verifiable regulatory judgement, not an operational productivity or performance metric.
Raymarine and maritime VTS results were measured on prototypes under controlled or synthetic conditions and are not production deployment results.
Raymarine and maritime VTS entries have small samples and no significance testing.
The maritime VTS timed percentages must not be averaged or combined into a single headline figure.
Some excluded engagements may have commercially significant evidence, but they do not meet the measured-outcome definition used on this page.
